title: A Lantern for the Letter
premise: In the winter of 1899, Marguerite Sandoval keeps the lantern at Pointe-Aubier, the last inhabited house before the tidal bridge that links her island to the mainland. When the great storms close the bridge for the season, she finds herself sheltering Elias Brandt, a German cartographer who once saved her late husband's life and to whom a promise of refuge was made in peacetime — but Brandt is now, by decree and by rumor, an enemy of the republic. As suspicion hardens among the islanders and a government inspector arrives with the thaw, Marguerite must choose between the law, her neighbors, and the debt of a dead man. The novel ends at the century's turning: Marguerite lights the lantern one last time as keeper, having smuggled Brandt out on the first ferry, and accepts the inspector's quiet bargain — her post surrendered, her conscience intact — finding belonging not in the tower she loses but in the community that finally claims her.
about_author: Odile Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing coastal lighthouse logs from the Atlantic seaboard. She writes historical fiction about ordinary people caught in history's machinery, and lives within sight of a decommissioned light.

chapters.title: The Last Ferry
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In October 1899, Marguerite tends the Pointe-Aubier light alone, convinced history belongs to capitals and newspapers, not to her rock. She sees off the last autumn ferry carrying her daughter to school on the mainland. The beat is quiet loneliness disguised as contentment — the calm before the season closes in.

chapters.title: A Stranger on the Rocks
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A storm wrecks a small boat below the tower; among the wreckage Marguerite pulls out Elias Brandt, half-drowned, clutching a waterproof satchel of maps. She recognizes him from her husband's letters — the man who pulled Henri from a canal in peacetime. The beat: reluctant duty awakening old grief.

chapters.title: What Henri Promised
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. Recovering in the keeper's quarters, Brandt reveals he came seeking Marguerite deliberately: Henri promised him refuge if ever he needed it, and now his name appears on a government list. He carries maps the navy wants — and others want destroyed. The beat: the weight of a promise made by a man who cannot keep it.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The great storms arrive early; the tidal bridge floods and the authorities seal it until spring. No one leaves, no one arrives — except word travels by wire: there is an enemy on the island. The beat: claustrophobia as geography becomes prison, and Marguerite realizes she has chosen her side by silence.

chapters.title: Neighbors
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The islanders — fisherman Tomas, shopkeeper Madame Roux, the priest — begin asking questions; someone saw a stranger's smoke. Marguerite lies badly, then learns Brandt has been quietly mending nets and fixing roofs, earning grudging tolerance. The beat: belonging tested — is he theirs yet, or never?

chapters.title: The Inspector's Wire
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. A telegram announces Inspector Lefèvre will cross at the first break in the weather, weeks ahead of the thaw. Brandt prepares to flee by sea in a repaired skiff; Marguerite argues the winter sea is death. Their argument cracks into confession — her guilt over Henri, his shame over what his own country made him. The beat: two people bound by a dead man's word.

chapters.title: Fire on the Water
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Sabotage: the skiff burns at its mooring, and suspicion falls on the islanders themselves — or was it Brandt destroying evidence? Tomas confronts Marguerite with the newspaper list bearing Brandt's name. The beat: trust fracturing; the community turns inward and cruel, and Marguerite stands exposed as a liar.

chapters.title: The Long Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The worst storm of the year strikes; the light fails mid-blow and a fishing boat with three island boys runs dark toward the rocks. Marguerite and Brandt climb together into the gale to relight the lamp by hand, saving the boat. The beat: climax of shared labor — the enemy's hands keeping the island's children alive.

chapters.title: Inspector Lefèvre
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. The ice breaks; Lefèvre crosses to find a hero story already forming around the relit lantern. Marguerite bargains openly: she will surrender her post and testify to nothing if the inspector looks away. Lefèvre, weary and pragmatic, agrees — power corrupts, but sometimes it can be spent mercifully. The beat: tense moral negotiation, resolution through sacrifice.

chapters.title: A Lantern for the Letter
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On New Year's Eve, the first ferry carries Brandt away with Henri's last letter in his coat; Marguerite lights the tower one final time before handing over the keys. The islanders, changed by the long night, offer her a cottage and a place among them. The beat: bittersweet resolution — inheritance redefined as belonging earned, not kept.
